result.summary: The gods meet on Olympus and Minerva persuades Jove to let Ulysses go home from Calypso's island. She visits Ithaca disguised as Mentes and urges Telemachus to confront the suitors and seek news of his father. Telemachus then asserts himself before his mother and the suitors.

scenes.title: Invocation and Ulysses' plight
scenes.summary: The poet asks the Muse to sing of Ulysses, whose men perished and who is held by Calypso.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses is kept from home and family by Calypso and Neptune's anger.

scenes.title: Council of the gods
scenes.summary: Jove blames Aegisthus' folly, and Minerva pleads for Ulysses. Jove explains Neptune's anger and they resolve to send Mercury to Calypso while Minerva goes to Ithaca.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses may never reach home while Neptune's anger holds him back.

scenes.title: Minerva arrives as Mentes
scenes.summary: Disguised as Mentes, Minerva reaches Ulysses' house, where Telemachus welcomes her and seats her apart from the rowdy suitors.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus' household is being consumed by the suitors.

scenes.title: Mentes advises Telemachus
scenes.summary: Telemachus tells of the suitors' ravages; Mentes urges him to call an assembly and seek news at Pylos and Sparta, then flies off like a bird.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus risks losing his estate and life to the suitors.

scenes.title: Telemachus faces the suitors
scenes.summary: Telemachus rebukes Penelope's request to Phemius, then warns the suitors to leave. Antinous and Eurymachus answer him.
scenes.stakes: Telemachus risks the suitors' hostility by asserting his authority.

scenes.title: Night in the tower
scenes.summary: Euryclea lights Telemachus to bed, where he ponders his voyage all night.

notable_quotes.reason: Famous opening invocation of the Muse.
Telemachus' wry remark on knowing one's father.

analysis.text: Human folly versus divine responsibility opens the poem, with Aegisthus as a warning and Orestes as a model for Telemachus.
The hospitality scenes show the Greek custom of welcoming strangers, which the suitors violate.

legacy.text: The opening invocation of the Muse became a model for later epics such as Virgil's Aeneid.

fun_facts.text: This translation is Samuel Butler's prose version, with footnotes marked by numbers in the text.

language_notes.text: "Ingenious" renders the Greek epithet often translated "of many wiles"; Ulysses is famed for cunning and resourcefulness.
Ulysses' men slaughtered the Sun-god's sacred cattle on the island of Thrinacia, despite warnings; this episode is told later in the poem.
"He must needs" means he felt compelled to, or insisted on; it is archaic phrasing implying willful stubbornness.
"Neither here nor there" means beside the point; Minerva dismisses Aegisthus to turn the talk to Ulysses.
"Blandishment" means flattery or coaxing persuasion.
"Propitiate" means to win the favor of a god, here through sacrifice.
"Ogygian island" is Calypso's island, Ogygia.
"Redoubtable" means formidable, inspiring fear. "Quells" means subdues or crushes.
"Forthwith" means immediately, at once.
Draughts is the game now called checkers in America; the suitors pass time with it while consuming Ulysses' property.
"Damask" is a rich patterned fabric, here used as a cloth thrown over the seat.
A ewer is a large jug for water, used here to pour water over guests' hands before eating.
"Perforce" means by force or necessity; Phemius sings under compulsion, not by choice.
Telemachus means the suitors' feasting and the singer's music cost them nothing, since someone else, his household, pays for it all.
"Pray for longer legs" means they would wish to run away faster; wealth would be no use to them against Ulysses.
"It is a wise child that knows his own father" is a proverb: paternity can never be certain, voicing Telemachus' doubt and bitterness.
Poison for arrows: Ulysses sought a poison to tip his arrows. Ephyra was a city in northwestern Greece.
"Short shrift" means little time or mercy before punishment; the "sorry wedding" is a grim joke on the suitors' courting.
"Barrow" means a burial mound, the grave marker an honoured hero would receive.
Orestes killed Aegisthus to avenge his father Agamemnon, whom Aegisthus had murdered. He is held up as a model for Telemachus.
Cloisters here means the covered colonnade or porch around the courtyard of the house, not a monastery.
Hellas and middle Argos: Penelope means Greece broadly and the heart of the Peloponnese; Ulysses' fame spread across the Greek world.
Danaans is another name for the Greeks, like Achaeans, used in Homer for the Greek army at Troy.
"Speech is man's matter": public speaking and decisions belong to men; Telemachus asserts his authority as head of the household.
Spunging means sponging: living off another's hospitality without paying.
Hied is an archaic past tense of "hie", meaning hurried.
The price of twenty oxen shows Euryclea's high value; cattle were a standard measure of wealth.

context_notes.text: A hecatomb was a large sacrifice, originally of a hundred oxen. Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is god of the sea.
Aegisthus seduced Clytemnestra, wife of Agamemnon, and murdered Agamemnon on his return from Troy; Orestes later avenged his father.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is Ulysses' patron goddess and Jove's daughter. Jove (Zeus) is son of Saturn.
Telemachus is Ulysses' young son. The suitors are nobles courting Penelope and consuming the household's wealth while Ulysses is away.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) is goddess of wisdom and war. Olympus is the home of the gods; Ithaca is Ulysses' island kingdom.
The suitors are men courting Penelope, Ulysses' wife, assuming he is dead. They feast daily at his house, consuming his wealth.
Phemius is a bard who entertains the suitors at Ulysses' house, singing to the lyre.
Minerva is disguised as Mentes, a king of the Taphians, a seafaring people. Her disguise lets her advise Telemachus as a human friend of his father.
The suitors are nobles from Ithaca and nearby islands who court Penelope, Ulysses' wife, and consume his household's wealth while she delays choosing.
Nestor of Pylos and Menelaus of Sparta were Greek leaders at Troy who returned home earlier, so they might have news of Ulysses.
Phemius is the household bard. His song concerns the Greeks' troubled homecomings after Troy, when Minerva (the Greek Athena) punished them.
Antinous is the most arrogant of the suitors, who court Penelope and consume Ulysses' estate.
Telemachus repeats the name Mentes, the disguise Minerva used when she visited him, hiding the truth from the suitors.

literary_notes.text: The poet opens by calling on the Muse for inspiration, a conventional epic opening that also sets the hero as the subject.
Jove complains that mortals blame the gods for their own folly, yet the gods' own conduct is about to be debated, including Neptune's grudge.
"My heart bleeds" figures her sympathy as a physical wound, showing how deeply she feels for Ulysses.
Minerva's plan outlines the coming action: Telemachus's assembly, the suitors' challenge and his journey to Sparta and Pylos.
Descriptive phrases like "glittering golden sandals" and "bronze-shod spear" stress the goddess's divine power and status.
Telemachus' moody daydream of routing the suitors shows his helplessness, his longing for his father and his sense of justice.
"His unhappy father" and the row of his spears evoke the absent Ulysses and the household's sorrow.
Seating the guest apart from the noisy suitors sets Telemachus' courtesy against their insolence.
Minerva, who is speaking, knows Ulysses will return; she presents it as inspired guesswork, while the audience knows the truth.
Storm-winds "spirited him away" personifies the forces that took Ulysses, while "I inherit nothing but dismay" is a bitter irony on inheritance.
Minerva's picture of Ulysses armed at the threshold shows him as a formidable warrior and foreshadows his later return and revenge.
Minerva's departure "like a bird" hints at her divinity, and her sudden flight shows who the visitor really was.
Telemachus speaks with new firmness, correcting his mother publicly; Minerva's visit has visibly changed him from the passive youth he was.
The threat that suitors will fall in Ulysses' house anticipates their eventual slaughter at his return.
Biting lips vividly conveys the suitors' suppressed anger and surprise at his boldness.
The narrator reveals Telemachus knows the goddess was his guest, while the suitors remain deceived by his answer.
